JSP vs Servlet?

A servlet is Java code that writes out HTML, so it's good for controller logic. A JSP is HTML with embedded tags, so it's good for the view. Every JSP is translated into a servlet. JSPs are recompiled automatically when they change.
Name the 9 JSP implicit objects.
request, response, out (JspWriter), session, application (ServletContext), config (ServletConfig), pageContext, page (this), exception (only available in error pages).
What are JSP directives?

- <%@ page %>: page settings: import, contentType, session, errorPage, isErrorPage, isELIgnored.
- <%@ include file="" %>: a static include, merged at translation time.
- <%@ taglib %>: declares a tag library such as JSTL or custom tags.
Include directive vs <jsp:include> action?

<%@ include file %> | <jsp:include page />
Translation time (static) | Request time (dynamic)
Content is merged into a single servlet | A separate resource is called at runtime
A change to the included file may not be picked up | Always the latest output; can take params
Scripting elements: scriptlet, expression, declaration?

<% code %> is a scriptlet and goes into _jspService. <%= expr %> is an expression and is printed to out. <%! decl %> is a declaration and becomes a class-level field or method. Avoid scriptlets: they mix logic into the view and are hard to maintain. Use EL and JSTL instead.
What are the four JSP scopes?
page (the current JSP) < request (one request, survives a forward) < session (one user) < application (the whole app). EL searches them in that order: ${user}.
What is EL and JSTL?

EL (Expression Language): ${expr} reads beans and scoped attributes, e.g. ${param.id}, ${sessionScope.cart.size()}, and returns null instead of throwing NPEs. JSTL is the standard tag library: core (c:if, c:forEach, c:choose, c:url), fmt (i18n and formatting), functions (fn:length), sql, xml.
How to handle exceptions in JSP?

Set <%@ page errorPage="error.jsp" %> on the page and isErrorPage="true" on error.jsp, which gives it access to exception. Or configure it globally in web.xml with <error-page> by exception type or status code.
Is JSP still used? What replaced it?

It's mostly legacy now. New server-side rendering uses Thymeleaf (the usual choice with Spring Boot, which has no default), FreeMarker, or SPA front ends (Angular, React) talking to REST APIs. Spring Boot's support for JSP with an embedded JAR is limited (you need WAR packaging).
Output: what do two consecutive requests print? <%! int hits = 0; %><% int local = 0; hits++; local++; %>hits=<%= hits %> local=<%= local %>

hits=1 local=1, then hits=2 local=1 (run on Tomcat 11). The declaration is an instance field of the single generated servlet, so it persists, while the scriptlet variable is a local of _jspService. hits is also unsafe under concurrency, and it resets on recompilation or redeploy.
Why can't you use request or session inside a declaration?

Implicit objects are local variables of _jspService, and a declaration is placed at class level, outside that method. A method declared in <%! %> must receive them as parameters. Only scriptlets and expressions see them directly.
Can you override _jspService()? What about jspInit()?

You can't override _jspService, because the translator generates that method from the page, so writing your own creates a duplicate. jspInit and jspDestroy can be overridden inside a declaration. Use them for one-time setup.
Does a JSP run on every request? Is it recompiled every time?

The compiled servlet runs on every request, but translation happens only the first time or when the file changes. Whether changes are checked depends on Jasper's development and checkInterval settings. Compiled code means it's no slower than a hand-written servlet after the first hit.
Translation-time vs request-time errors?

Translation-time: bad JSP syntax, a missing tag library, a bad directive, an unclosed tag. Compile-time: errors in Java inside scriptlets, or using session when session="false" (Tomcat 11 said "session cannot be resolved"). Request-time: runtime exceptions such as an EL PropertyNotFoundException. The first two return 500 with a JasperException and don't reach the page's errorPage.
What does session="false" do, and when would you use it?

The page no longer creates or touches an HTTP session, and the session implicit object doesn't exist. Use it on public pages such as a landing page, so that crawlers and anonymous visitors don't each cost a session in server memory. Note that it doesn't invalidate an existing session.
What's the output of ${10/2}, ${1/0}, ${"1"+"2"} and ${null+1}?

5.0, Infinity, 3 and 1, verified on Tomcat 11. EL division is floating-point, so dividing by zero doesn't throw. + always means numeric addition, with strings coerced to numbers and null to 0. A non-numeric string in + fails: ${"a"+1} raised NumberFormatException on Tomcat 11. Concatenate with += or by placing expressions side by side.
What does EL print when a value is null, compared with an expression?

EL prints an empty string. A scriptlet expression prints the word null: in a test, <%= request.getAttribute("n") %>|${n}| printed null||. EL also ignores null in a chain: ${nothing.x.y} prints nothing. But an existing bean without the property throws PropertyNotFoundException.
Why doesn't ${request.method} work?

request is a JSP implicit object, not an EL one, so EL looks for an attribute called request, doesn't find it, and prints nothing. Use ${pageContext.request.method}. In the test, ${pageContext.request.contextPath} printed /app and ${pageContext.request.method} printed GET.
What does empty check? How is it different from == null?

empty x is true if x is null, an empty String, or an empty array, Collection or Map. x == null is true only for null: ${"" == null} is false. It's the right check for lists: <c:if test="${not empty orders}">.
How do you access a request parameter, a header and a cookie in EL?

${param.id}, or ${paramValues.id[1]} for a repeated param; ${header['user-agent']}, with brackets because of the hyphen; and ${cookie.theme.value}, because cookie.theme is the Cookie object. ${cookie.theme} alone would print its toString().
c:out vs ${}: when must you use which?

Use <c:out> or fn:escapeXml for any data that a user could have influenced. Plain ${} is fine only for values known to be safe (numbers, your own constants). Otherwise a name of <script>...</script> executes in other users' browsers. Note that it escapes for HTML only. Inside JavaScript or a URL you need encoding for that context (c:url with c:param, or the OWASP Java Encoder).
How do you implement if/else in JSTL?
c:if has no else branch. Use c:choose, c:when, c:otherwise, which works as if / else-if / else, stopping at the first true when. For a one-liner, use a ternary: ${active ? 'On' : 'Off'}.
What's varStatus?

An object that describes the current iteration of c:forEach: index (from 0), count (from 1), first, last, current, plus begin, end and step. It's useful for zebra rows: ${s.count % 2 == 0 ? 'even' : 'odd'}.
What does c:url do that a plain link doesn't?

It prepends the context path to paths beginning with /, URL-encodes c:param values, and adds ;jsessionid= if the client hasn't shown cookie support. In the test, /x with param q="a b" gave /app/x;jsessionid=...?q=a+b on a first request. Without it, moving the app to a different context breaks hard-coded links.
jsp:forward vs response.sendRedirect from a JSP?

Same difference as in servlets. jsp:forward stays on the server, so the request attributes and URL are kept, and buffered output is dropped. It must happen before commit. Page content after it doesn't run, because the generated code returns. sendRedirect makes the browser issue a new request. In a scriptlet, follow it with return; or the rest of the page still executes.
Does the included file get its own scope with jsp:include? Does a param passed by jsp:param stay?

The target gets a new page scope, so page attributes aren't visible there, but it shares the request and session. jsp:param values are added to the request for the duration of the include: ${param.x} worked in the target, and they disappear when control returns. If the same name already exists, the new value takes precedence.
A shared header is changed and included by a static include directive. Will pages show it?

The content was pasted into each page at translation, so each one must be retranslated. Tomcat tracks these dependencies in development mode and recompiles. Other containers or production settings with no checks may keep the old output until redeployed. Runtime includes avoid this.
How do you disable scriptlets across an application?

<scripting-invalid>true</scripting-invalid> inside a jsp-property-group in web.xml, with <url-pattern>*.jsp</url-pattern>. Pages containing scripting elements then fail at translation. That enforces the "no Java in views" rule, so a code review doesn't have to.
Why put JSPs under WEB-INF?

Files under WEB-INF can't be requested from a browser, only reached by a forward. That guarantees the controller runs first, so security checks happen and model data exists. Otherwise a direct hit on orders.jsp renders an empty page or an error.
What are classic tag return values, and how do they control the body?

doStartTag returns EVAL_BODY_INCLUDE (process the body) or SKIP_BODY. doAfterBody returns EVAL_BODY_AGAIN (loop) or SKIP_BODY. doEndTag returns EVAL_PAGE or SKIP_PAGE, the latter stopping the rest of the JSP. BodyTag adds EVAL_BODY_BUFFERED to capture the body. SimpleTag replaced all this with one doTag and getJspBody().invoke().
What's the purpose of a TLD?

A Tag Library Descriptor is an XML file that tells the translator the tag names, handler classes, attributes, and which attributes are required or accept expressions (rtexprvalue). It's used to validate tag usage at translation time. Containers find TLDs under WEB-INF and in META-INF of library JARs, which is why JSTL works with only a URI. Tag files in /WEB-INF/tags need no TLD.
Is a JSP thread-safe?

Exactly as much as a servlet, because it is one. Scriptlet locals and page scope are safe. Declarations (<%! %>), session attributes and application attributes are shared. isThreadSafe="false" is deprecated and was never a true fix. Avoid declaring mutable fields.
How would you handle internationalisation in JSP?

Create messages.properties, messages_de.properties and so on, on the classpath. Load with fmt:setBundle, or set the jakarta.servlet.jsp.jstl.fmt.localizationContext context param. Print text with <fmt:message key="..."/>, and pass arguments using fmt:param. The locale comes from fmt:setLocale or the browser's Accept-Language. Use UTF-8 for pageEncoding, and format numbers and dates with fmt:formatNumber and fmt:formatDate because they differ by locale.
How do you migrate a legacy JSP/Struts app to a modern stack?

- Characterise behaviour with end-to-end tests first.
- Move logic from scriptlets into services, and add Spring MVC controllers in front, so JSPs become pure views.
- Replace views in stages with Thymeleaf, or expose REST endpoints for an Angular or React front end, using a strangler approach where a proxy routes migrated paths to the new app.
- Upgrade javax to jakarta together with the Spring Boot upgrade. JSTL URIs and library versions change too.
- Decide whether to keep WAR packaging until the last JSP has gone.
A JSP shows raw ${...} text in the browser. Why?

EL is off for that page. Causes: isELIgnored="true"; a matching <el-ignored> in web.xml; or an old web.xml with a Servlet 2.3 DTD, which ignores EL by default. Another case: the file isn't being processed at all, such as a .html file or a static template served by the default servlet.
Why do blank lines appear in generated HTML, and does it matter?

Each directive or scriptlet line leaves its newline in the template text. It's mostly harmless for HTML, but it breaks a page that must output plain JSON or XML starting at the first byte, or a file download. Fix it with trimDirectiveWhitespaces="true", or better, don't produce non-HTML from a JSP. A cause of "getOutputStream() has already been called" is using a JSP for binary output, since the page's out uses the writer.
What does the Spring form tag library give you over plain HTML inputs?

Binding: path="name" reads and writes the property of the modelAttribute object, so values are redisplayed after a validation error; <form:errors> prints BindingResult messages; select/checkbox tags handle selected state; values are HTML-escaped; and with Spring Security the CSRF token is inserted automatically.
Why does a POST from my JSP return 403 after adding Spring Security?

CSRF protection is on by default and the form didn't send the token. Use <form:form>, or add <input type="hidden" name="${_csrf.parameterName}" value="${_csrf.token}"/> to plain forms. For AJAX calls, put the token in a meta tag and send it in the X-CSRF-TOKEN header.
How do you show a "saved successfully" message after a redirect in a JSP app?

Use Post/Redirect/Get with a flash attribute: in the controller call redirectAttributes.addFlashAttribute("msg", "Saved") and return "redirect:/list". Spring stores it in the session for exactly one following request and exposes it as a model attribute, so the JSP prints ${msg} (escaped with c:out). Request attributes wouldn't survive the redirect, and plain session attributes would linger.
How does a controller's return value map to a JSP?

The InternalResourceViewResolver (or Spring Boot's spring.mvc.view.prefix/suffix) turns the logical view name into a path, for example prefix /WEB-INF/views/ + home + .jsp. The DispatcherServlet copies model attributes into request attributes and forwards to that JSP. A redirect: or forward: prefix bypasses the resolver.
JSP vs JSF?

JSP is a template technology that is translated into a servlet and renders whatever the controller prepared. JSF (Jakarta Faces) is a component-based MVC framework with a component tree, lifecycle phases, managed beans and Facelets (XHTML) views; it keeps UI state across requests. JSF is found in older enterprise/Java EE apps; new projects mostly use Thymeleaf or a SPA with REST.
